thread.title: 'Unity Against Empire' explores U.S. Black and Latine activism
thread.title_full: 'Unity Against Empire' explores U.S. Black and Latine activism

author: Elizabeth Rozeboom
title: 'Unity Against Empire' explores U.S. Black and Latine activism
text:
On Tuesday evening, students and community members gathered in the School of Education for “Unity Against Empire: Black and Latine Solidarity in Struggle,” a Black History Month teach-in. The event highlighted the history of Black and Latine protest movements by focusing on pioneer groups including the Black Panther Party, Young Lords Organization and the Rainbow Coalition.
Solidaridad Organizada para la Liberación, a Latine activist student organization at the University, hosted the event in collaboration with the General Defense Committee, All-African People’s Revolutionary Party, Community Movement Builders and Michigan Action for Cuba Committee.
In an interview with The Michigan Daily, Rackham student Nia Hall, SOL political education chair, said the teach-in was intended to provide a space for conversation.
“We wanted to do a teach-in with a documentary to really educate our community on the history of our activism,” Hall said. “We wanted to provide a really low-key space for folks to come in, have food and learn together.”
Hall began the event with a brief historical background on the activist groups and the purpose behind learning about them.
“It’s a political memory exercise,” Hall said. “For us to be able to remember our history and our history of struggle and unity and solidarity … Tonight’s documentary shows one moment where ordinary people decided that they would not wait for permission to survive.”
The event continued with a documentary screening about the Young Lords’ 1970 takeover of Lincoln Hospital in New York City. In an interview with The Daily, LSA junior Emma Sital said the teach-in was a great educational opportunity on historical events.
“I thought it was really amazing,” Sital said. “I had never heard of the hospital takeover of the Young Lords. So, to me, this was a really cool learning experience.”
The event wrapped up with a discussion about the impact of activism movements on society and how lasting change occurs when people come together and push into new avenues of resistance. Hall encouraged audience members to support the ongoing Michigan Action for Cuba 2026 medicine drive for Cuban citizens during the country’s current health care blockade.
Sital told The Daily she believes the historical takeovers of the Young Lords parallels some recent activism at the University of Michigan, like the 2024 Gaza solidarity encampment.
“I think it definitely has parallels to what has happened, at least, within my time at (the University of) Michigan relating to encampments,” Sital said. “And the concept of occupying space — I can see a lot of similarities. I think they mirror each other in terms of intention.”
In an interview with The Daily, LSA senior Vanessa Rodriguez, an event attendee, said she wished there was the same present-day motivation for change as in the past.
“I’ve always been interested in the Black Panther Party and the Young Lords,” Rodriguez said. “I wish that we had more movements like those nowadays. I feel like they’ve been repressed for so long — that’s why we don’t see as much now.”
Rodriguez said she particularly enjoyed the inspirational conversations she had with other attendees.
“My highlight was hearing such good discussion after the documentary,” Rodriguez said. “I appreciated how much people contributed. It makes me feel motivated to have so many people also motivated to doing more, for the movement and for the communities.”
Daily News Contributor Elizabeth Rozeboom can be reached at elizaroz@umich.edu.
